What is the essential teaching in 'The Buddha and His Dhamma'?

In 'The Buddha and His Dhamma', the teaching opens with this observation: *"Buddhism originated with an Indian prince known as the Buddha, who taught in Northeast India in the fifth century BC."* The central invitation is to turn one's investigation inward — to verify the Dhamma not as a set of beliefs, but as directly observable reality in one's own body, speech, and mind. As the text teaches, the Dhamma is *akāliko* — ever-present — and *opanayiko* — leading inward — available to be known (*paccattaṁ*) by each practitioner for themselves. There is no need to search elsewhere; the truth is already here.

Can you explain the teaching in the section '1. The Life of the Buddha'?

This section teaches: *"Although we cannot determine with absolute precision the dates of the Buddha's life, many scholars agree that he lived from approximately 563 to 483 BC; a growing number of scholars follow a different chronology which places the dates about eighty years later. As is natural with a spiritual leader who has made such a powerful impact on human civili..."* The core instruction is to turn investigation inward (*opanayiko*) toward what is already present in body, speech, and mind — not to seek the Dhamma outside or in future states. Whatever theme this section addresses, the method is the same: sustained, patient, non-grasping awareness that allows the truth to reveal itself. As Ajahn Mun taught: when the mind sees clearly, there is no longer any need to go looking.

This text mentions impermanence (anicca). Can you explain its role in practice?

In this text, anicca appears in this context: *"When she asked him for medicine, he did not give her an eloquent sermon on impermanence."* Understanding impermanence (anicca) is not merely conceptual — it is meant to be verified directly. The Dhamma is *ehipassiko*: 'come and see for yourself.' Bring the quality described by anicca into direct investigation: where is it present in your current experience? When seen clearly, each of these Pāli terms dissolves from abstract concept into living reality.

Why does the preceptor teach the five meditation themes at ordination?

The text explains: *"These must have been the questions that rippled across his mind, for we find his own reflections recorded for us in a discourse called "The Noble Quest" ( MN 26 ):
Monks, before my enlightenment, being myself subject to birth, aging, sickness and death, to sorrow and defilement, I sought what was subject to birth, aging, sickness and death, to sorrow and defilement."* The five themes — hair of head (kesā), hair of body (lomā), nails (nakhā), teeth (dantā), skin (taco) — are not arbitrary. They target the root of infatuation with the body. The skin, as the outermost layer, is what we are actually attracted to when we conceive of a body as beautiful. Contemplating the skin as a wrapping that holds together otherwise repulsive components directly undercuts sensual desire. This is the very first teaching given to a new monk — showing that the entire path begins with honest, unflinching investigation of the body.
